Former delivery drivers allege Mama Earth relocated to Mississauga to break up their union and fire dozens
Former Mama Earth Organics employees rallied outside the company's East York facility on April 21 to protest the loss of their jobs. (Submitted by Matt Davis - image credit)
Former employees of a Toronto-area subscription grocery service say the company used a warehouse relocation to Mississauga to carry out mass firings in an act of union-busting.
In March, dozens of Mama Earth Organics employees were told their jobs would end eight weeks later on May 12.
Matt Davis had been a delivery driver with the company for just under four years when he was handed his notice at work.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
“It told us that 101 people were getting terminated … that accounted for every hourly employee that was working there at that time,” Davis told CBC Toronto. “Looking around, everyone’s heads were just down. It was brutal.”
Mama Earth, a community-oriented organic food delivery company owned by Fresh City Farms, said the move to Mississauga followed plans to close its East York warehouse. Because the union’s collective agreement was limited to Toronto, the company was not required to carry it over, effectively separating the jobs from the unionized workforce.
Former Mama Earth Organics employees feel the company used a loophole in their collective agreement to carry out mass firings in an act of union-busting.
Former Mama Earth employees allege a warehouse move to Mississauga enabled mass job terminations for unionized staff. (Submitted by Matt Davis)
For Ian Goff, another former Mama Earth driver, the decision came as less of a shock than it did for some of his coworkers. “I’m disappointed, but I’m not surprised,” he told CBC Toronto. “It felt like it was kind of the climax … of a number of very anti-worker policies.”
He cited cameras installed in delivery vans, including in-cab cameras facing drivers during 10–12 hour shifts, as an example.
But Mama Earth CEO, Ran Goel, denied the move to Mississauga was intended to undermine the workers or union, saying it was driven by financial pressures.
Move to Mississauga driven by financial pressures: CEO
“We didn’t do this flippantly,” he told CBC Toronto. “We did it because we had to.”

He pointed to rising lease costs and over $1 million in required upgrades at the Toronto facility, including HVAC and refrigeration, and said other locations within Toronto did not meet requirements.
“Mama Earth should do the right thing and allow workers who wish to transfer to the new facility the opportunity to do so," Hanley wrote. "This supposed community-minded company should respect the dedication and service of our members who have contributed to the company’s success."

Mama Earth workers fight back against union busting
By Pedro García Contreras, Adam Lee
On Saturday, May 9th, laid-off workers at Toronto-based produce delivery service Mama Earth led a rally to protest union busting at their workplace.
The action comes on the heels of Mama Earth CEO Ran Goel’s announcement of the firing of 102 unionized workers, along with the business’ impending move from East York in Toronto to Mississauga.
Mass layoffs of unionized workers
In March, Goel informed employees at Mama Earth that the 102 unionized workers at its Waterman Ave warehouse would be laid off after eight weeks had passed. The non-unionized employees at the company, however, would be staying on board.
He also informed them that the Toronto warehouse where Mama Earth operates would be shutting down, and the warehouse would be moving to Mississauga.
Mass layoffs of unionized workers will always draw scrutiny, but the alarm was raised further by the warehouse’s change in location.
The collective agreement between Mama Earth and the union, UFCW 1006A, stipulates that the collective agreement would still apply within Toronto’s borders. However, the agreement has no language outlining what happens if the business moves outside of Toronto.
Workers allege that Mama Earth offered severance payments that only took into account time working at Mama Earth since the company merged with produce company Fresh City Farms and moved to the current facility at Waterman Ave.
Those who were working with Fresh City Farms prior to the merger and continued working with Mama Earth afterwards have not had their pre-merger service time included in the calculation of severance amounts, severely cutting into what the workers are owed.
Though Goel denies an anti-union motivation for these moves, his rhetoric is undermined by the fact that Mama Earth has since posted job listings looking to fill many of the roles previously filled by unionized workers.
As workers were quick to point out at Saturday’s rally, rehiring for the same jobs that were terminated and shifting to third-party services shows that those positions are not expendable, and keeping the non-union workers on board shows that Mama Earth is capable of retaining workers during the move — the only conceivable reason to fire the
unionized workers is to bust the union.
“What’s disgusting? Union busting!”
Standing outside the Mama Earth warehouse in East York with signs and leaflets, workers and supporters led chants, the most popular being the classic: “What’s disgusting? Union busting!”
mirrors.
Tuesday, May 12th, is the last day Mama Earth Workers are slated to work at the Waterman Ave location, but they plan on continuing to fight for their rights regardless of where the warehouse is located.

Environmental Current Events 2026
News on sustainable communities, scientific findings, the push toward net-zero carbon emissions, and more!
By MOTHER EARTH NEWS
| Published on February 17, 2026
[Email](mailto:?subject=Environmental Current Events 2026&body=https://www.motherearthnews.com/sustainable-living/environmental-current-events-zm0z26zols/) Print Facebook
Walk through the orchard today, and you won’t see any bare soil, but instead a flourishing understory of perennial grasses and legumes grazed by sheep.
These days, lowering the cost of synthetic fertilizer can be a make-or-break move for a farm: As of March 2026, the cost of both urea-based and anhydrous fertilizers had risen upward of 35 percent over the previous month, to $800 per ton and $1,000 per ton, respectively.
Daley is co-founder of the Center for Regenerative Agriculture and Resilient Systems at California State University, Chico, where she’s studied regenerative agriculture for 20 years.
“Regenerative systems can reduce synthetic nitrogen applications between 30 and 80 percent, depending on climate, soil type, and management intensity,” she says, noting that some farmers can eliminate synthetic inputs altogether. Daley cites a 2021 study of Montes’ almond orchard led by researcher Jonathan Lundgren.
Lundgren found that, compared with conventional farm soils, Montes’ regeneratively managed soils contained a third more carbon and 19% more nitrogen, as well as more phosphorus, calcium, and sulfur.
“What’s happening is that you’re shifting from a system that depends on applied nitrogen to one that’s doing a better job of cycling and holding on to nutrients,” Daley says.
Daley appreciates the various certification programs that have emerged for regenerative ag, but she doesn’t get caught up in strict definitions.
“If what you’re doing is improving soil health, increasing biological activity, building soil carbon, and making your farm more resilient over time, then you’re moving in a regenerative direction,” she says.
Still, several practices are regenerative mainstays: reducing tillage, never leaving bare soil, maximizing plant (and soil) diversity, integrating livestock, and, ultimately, reducing synthetic agrochemicals. A unifying force between them is maintaining ground cover, which Lundgren’s study suggests is the primary driver of increased soil carbon.
By reducing imported fertilizers, as well as decreasing irrigation and introducing income streams from integrated livestock, regenerative systems can make farms more profitable by 78 percent or more.
Fruits and Vegetables Rx
The system draws on the Earth’s constant subterranean temperatures (about 55 to 60 degrees F in many places) to absorb heat in winter and offload it in summer – achieving an astonishing 400 percent efficiency or better.
